executive_summary: This assessment reviews the status of Pratt & Whitney (RTX) powder metal manufacturing defects and their impact on the Airbus A320neo fleet, based on SEC filings and FAA regulatory directives published between February and October 2026. Evidence includes RTX quarterly and annual reports [DOC_013, DOC_014, DOC_015, DOC_017] and FAA Airworthiness Directives (AD) [DOC_006, DOC_018]. The monitored scope confirms that a "rare condition in powder metal" used for engine parts requires "accelerated inspection of the PW1100G-JM (PW1100) GTF fleet" [DOC_017]. Regulatory findings confirm that the FAA mandated repetitive angled ultrasonic inspections (AUSIs) for high-pressure turbine (HPT) 1st-stage disks and turbine hubs, effective June 26, 2026 [DOC_006, DOC_018]. While issuer filings acknowledge increased "aircraft on ground levels" (AOG) and costs [DOC_017], specific global AOG counts and precise compliance deadlines for the broader fleet remain missing from the available disclosures. Management should focus on quantifying the delta between the 430 engines identified in U.S. registry impacts [DOC_006] and the total global fleet requirements to refine capacity planning for shop visits.
detailed_analytical_assessment:
The technical quality issue stems from powder metal contamination affecting critical engine components, specifically HPT disks and HPC 7th-stage integrally bladed rotors. According to RTX disclosures, Pratt & Whitney determined in July 2023 that this condition necessitated an accelerated inspection schedule for the PW1100G-JM engines powering the Airbus A320neo family [DOC_017]. By early 2026, the company reported that this "Powder Metal Matter" continued to drive increased engine removals, shop visits, and AOG levels [DOC_013, DOC_017]. 

Regulatory intervention solidified in mid-2026. An official record dated April 24, 2026, detailed requirements for repetitive AUSIs to detect crack indications, noting that the U.S. registry impact alone involved approximately 430 engines [DOC_006]. A subsequent FAA publication on May 22, 2026, established an effective date of June 26, 2026, for AD 2026-10360, which also covers PW4000 series models (PW4074 through PW4090) [DOC_018]. Analytically, the expansion of the AD to include PW4000 models suggests the powder metal issue may have broader implications across Pratt & Whitney’s product lines than initially reported for the GTF fleet alone.

Despite these findings, significant data gaps persist. While RTX filings through October 2026 [DOC_013] maintain the same descriptive language regarding the "rare condition," they do not provide updated global AOG metrics or specific recovery timelines for the A320neo fleet. The relationship between the IAE LLC collaboration (Pratt & Whitney, JAEC, and MTU) is confirmed as the vehicle for product support [DOC_015], but the specific division of financial and technical liability for the 2026 inspection surge is not fully detailed. Management is advised to monitor for supplemental FAA notices that may adjust inspection intervals based on initial AUSI findings and to seek secondary verification of shop visit throughput at IAE facilities to gauge the duration of AOG impacts.

kiq_answers.question: What is the current regulatory status and compliance timeline for the PW1100G powdered metal High Pressure Turbine (HPT) and High Pressure Compressor (HPC) disk inspections?
kiq_answers.answer: Reviewed sources address part of this question, while specific verification items remain open. FAA publication 2026-10360, published 2026-05-22; stage EFFECTIVE; effective date 2026-06-26; effective as of 2026-11-25: TRUE. Later amendments and supersession have not been verified. An official regulatory record on 2026-04-24 notes that “This AD requires repetitive angled ultrasonic inspections (AUSIs) of certain high-pressure turbine (HPT) 1st-stage disks and turbine hubs for any crack indications, and if necessary, removal from service…” [DOC_006]. An official regulatory record on 2026-05-22 notes that “Effective Date: 2026-06-26” [DOC_018]. An official regulatory record on 2026-05-22 notes that “The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Pratt & Whitney RTX Corporation (PW) Model PW4074, PW4074D, PW4077, PW4077D, PW4084D, PW4090, and PW4090-3 engines. This AD was prompted by an analysis…” [DOC_018]. Evidence establishes identity of the affected part or engine, specific inspection or required corrective action, direct applicability to the named model or program, whereas latest dated, issue-specific status still require direct confirmation. run_metadata.editor_executive_summary: This assessment reviews the status of Pratt & Whitney (RTX) powder metal manufacturing defects and their impact on the Airbus A320neo fleet, based on SEC filings and FAA regulatory directives published between February and October 2026. Evidence includes RTX quarterly and annual reports [DOC_013, DOC_014, DOC_015, DOC_017] and FAA Airworthiness Directives (AD) [DOC_006, DOC_018]. The monitored scope confirms that a "rare condition in powder metal" used for engine parts requires "accelerated inspection of the PW1100G-JM (PW1100) GTF fleet" [DOC_017]. Regulatory findings confirm that the FAA mandated repetitive angled ultrasonic inspections (AUSIs) for high-pressure turbine (HPT) 1st-stage disks and turbine hubs, effective June 26, 2026 [DOC_006, DOC_018]. While issuer filings acknowledge increased "aircraft on ground levels" (AOG) and costs [DOC_017], specific global AOG counts and precise compliance deadlines for the broader fleet remain missing from the available disclosures. Management should focus on quantifying the delta between the 430 engines identified in U.S. registry impacts [DOC_006] and the total global fleet requirements to refine capacity planning for shop visits.
run_metadata.editor_detailed_analytical_assessment:
The technical quality issue stems from powder metal contamination affecting critical engine components, specifically HPT disks and HPC 7th-stage integrally bladed rotors. According to RTX disclosures, Pratt & Whitney determined in July 2023 that this condition necessitated an accelerated inspection schedule for the PW1100G-JM engines powering the Airbus A320neo family [DOC_017]. By early 2026, the company reported that this "Powder Metal Matter" continued to drive increased engine removals, shop visits, and AOG levels [DOC_013, DOC_017]. 

Regulatory intervention solidified in mid-2026. An official record dated April 24, 2026, detailed requirements for repetitive AUSIs to detect crack indications, noting that the U.S. registry impact alone involved approximately 430 engines [DOC_006]. A subsequent FAA publication on May 22, 2026, established an effective date of June 26, 2026, for AD 2026-10360, which also covers PW4000 series models (PW4074 through PW4090) [DOC_018]. Analytically, the expansion of the AD to include PW4000 models suggests the powder metal issue may have broader implications across Pratt & Whitney’s product lines than initially reported for the GTF fleet alone.

Despite these findings, significant data gaps persist. While RTX filings through October 2026 [DOC_013] maintain the same descriptive language regarding the "rare condition," they do not provide updated global AOG metrics or specific recovery timelines for the A320neo fleet. The relationship between the IAE LLC collaboration (Pratt & Whitney, JAEC, and MTU) is confirmed as the vehicle for product support [DOC_015], but the specific division of financial and technical liability for the 2026 inspection surge is not fully detailed. Management is advised to monitor for supplemental FAA notices that may adjust inspection intervals based on initial AUSI findings and to seek secondary verification of shop visit throughput at IAE facilities to gauge the duration of AOG impacts.
